subject: Biotechnology
title: The $1000 Genome
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The $1000 Genome.

hook.text: The Human Genome Project cost $2.7 billion — today sequencing a genome costs under $200. Price collapse changed everything.

buildup.text: Illumina's sequencing-by-synthesis reads millions of DNA fragments simultaneously — massively parallel processing.

discovery.text: Cheaper sequencing democratized genomics — hospitals, startups, and even consumers can now read their DNA.

twist.text: Sequencing is cheap but interpretation is expensive — understanding what variants mean still requires expert analysis.

climax.text: Nanopore sequencing fits in your palm — the MinION reads DNA in real time, even in remote field locations.

punchline.text: Read a genome for the price of an MRI — sequencing is now routine medicine.

quiz.question: Why hasn't cheap genome sequencing immediately improved healthcare for everyone?
options: Most people do not have enough DNA to sequence
Interpreting what genetic variants mean still requires expensive expert analysis
Sequencing machines are too large for hospitals to install

details.summary: The prospect of sequencing individual human genomes for under 1,000 dollars has become reality, making comprehensive genomic analysis affordable for routine clinical use.

takeaways: Whole genome sequencing costs have fallen below 1,000 dollars per genome
Cost reduction makes population-scale genomic medicine economically feasible
The Illumina NovaSeq and MGI platforms drove costs below this threshold

faq.question: How did genome sequencing costs drop so dramatically?
faq.answer: The Human Genome Project cost about 3 billion dollars. Sequencing costs decreased a millionfold through massively parallel sequencing technology, where millions of DNA fragments are read simultaneously. Illumina's flow cell and chemistry innovations were the primary drivers of cost reduction.

faq.question: Is a 1,000 dollar genome sufficient for clinical diagnosis?
faq.answer: The sequencing cost is just one component. Interpretation, data storage, clinical reporting, and genetic counseling add significant costs. However, the sequencing cost milestone means the technology itself is no longer the barrier. Integration into healthcare workflows is the remaining challenge.
